skill.name: An ending that lands
skill.why: The ending is what readers remember. Make it worth the trip.
skill.how: Solve the problem, show how the character has changed, or circle back to the start.

steps.say: Tully's story starts: 'Tully never passed the ball to anyone.' Now it needs an ending.

show.text: Then everyone went home for tea.
show.nudge: That's just the next thing that happened. Is anything different about Tully?

show.text: With one second left, Tully passed to Mo, and he kicked the goal.

show.nudge: It just stops. Did anything about Tully change?

steps.ask: Tap the ending that feels finished.
steps.win: Yes! It feels finished, like a perfect landing after a jump. Writers say an ending like that lands.

steps.say: Why does it work? Put the first line and the last line side by side.

show.text: Tully never passed the ball to anyone.

steps.ask: What is different about Tully at the end?

options.reason: The story never says that. Look at what she does with the ball.
She's still a player. What does she do that she never did before?

steps.win: Yes! At the start she never passed. At the end she does. Tully has changed.

steps.say: Here's another way. This story starts: 'The bin was growling.' Look for a link at the end.

show.text: The bin went to the tip.
show.nudge: That is an ending, but does it link back? Say the first line again.
It doesn't link back to the start. Which one is about the bin's noise?

steps.ask: Tap the ending that links back to the first line.
steps.win: Yes! Growling at the start, purring at the end. Going back to the start is a callback.

steps.say: Or end on a picture the reader can still see after the story ends.

show.text: It was a good day, and I was happy.
show.nudge: Good and happy are telling words. Can you see anything?

show.text: The last firefly blinked once, then flew out to sea.
Then we all went to bed.
show.nudge: It's true, but there's nothing to picture. Which one can you see?

steps.ask: Tap the ending you can see in your head.
steps.win: Yes! You can see that firefly. A last picture stays with the reader after the story ends.

steps.say: Zed ends every story like this. He says it is a great surprise.

show.text: Then I woke up. It was all a dream.

steps.ask: What does a dream ending do to the story?

options.reason: If it was a dream, the problem never happened. Was anything really solved?

options.text: It shows how the character changed.
options.reason: Nobody changed. They just woke up. Did any of it count?

steps.win: Right. It feels like a cheat. Writers say an ending like that falls flat. Lucky surprises do the same.

steps.say: In my story, a possum is stuck in a drainpipe. The ending that solves it is the resolution.

show.text: A possum was stuck in the drainpipe.

options.text: Suddenly the possum grew wings and flew out.
options.reason: Where did wings come from? I didn't do anything, so I didn't earn it.

options.text: Then I woke up in my bed.
options.reason: A dream ending. It cancels the whole rescue.

options.text: I built a ramp from an old plank, and the possum climbed out.

steps.win: Yes! I did it myself, so I earned it. Now land your story: a change, a callback or a picture.

terms.means: The character does something they never did at the start.
The last line links back to the first line.
A last picture the reader can still see after the story ends.
A dream or a lucky surprise. It cancels the story.

examples.text: Tully, who never passed to anyone, handed Mo the ball.

card.test: Read your first and last lines together. Is the problem solved? Has someone changed, or does it link back?

weDo.frame: Wren's story starts: 'Mo's cooking had never won a single prize.'
weDo.hint: Which one links back to the first line?
weDo.success: It circles back to the prize, shows Mo finally won, and the gravy keeps it funny.

options.text: Mo held up the blue ribbon. It was covered in gravy, and he didn't care one bit.
Everyone packed up and went home, and Mo had a big bowl of ice cream for dinner.
options.reason: It just stops. It never goes back to Mo's cooking or whether he won a prize.

options.text: In the end, Mo learned that if you try really hard, you can do anything.
options.reason: It tells a lesson, but we never find out if Mo's cooking won a prize.

weDo.frame: Wren's story about Zed starts: 'Zed always quit when he lost.'
weDo.prompt: Tap the ending that falls flat. Then choose one that lands.
weDo.hint: Look back at the first line. What has Zed always done?
weDo.success: Zed always quit. Now he plays on. The ending shows he has changed.

parts.tap: In the last round, Zed was losing again.
parts.reason: This keeps the problem going, so it stays. Find the last line that cheats.
Shaking thumbs show he's nervous. That's good. Find the line that cancels the story.

parts.tap: Then he woke up, and it was all a dream.

options.text: Zed took a deep breath and pressed play one more time.
Suddenly the power went out, so nobody won at all.
options.reason: Luck ends it, not Zed. Nobody earned that ending.

options.text: In the end, Zed realised that quitting is never the answer.
options.reason: It tells us Zed changed, but we never see him do anything different.

creature.name: Swoopet
creature.blurb: An owl that circles the whole bay at night, then lands without a sound on the very branch it left from.

workshop.mentor:
By the time we reached the jetty, my torch had run flat. I didn't need it any more.
Six months ago, I wouldn't walk to the letterbox after dark. Tonight I had carried a sleepy Creature through a cave full of bats.
I opened the shoebox, and the little glow-worm floated out over the water. Then I walked back up the hill in the dark, and I didn't hurry.
workshop.ask:
Write the last four sentences of Gus's slime story, or your own.
Stuck? Start with: 'The slime was still singing when...'
Challenge: echo your first line in your last.
checklist: My last lines solve the main problem.
I can point to a line that shows a change.
My last line echoes my first, or leaves a picture.
No dream and no luck: my character fixes it.
